prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

“A true Arab knows how to catch a fly in his hands,” my father would say. And he’d prove it, cupping the buzzer instantly while the host with the swatter stared. In the spring our palms peeled like snakes. True Arabs believed watermelon could heal fifty ways. I changed these to fit the occasion. Years before, a girl knocked, wanted to see the Arab. I said we didn’t have one. After that, my father told me who he was, “Shihab”—“shooting star”— a good name, borrowed from the sky. Once I said, “When we die, we give it back?” He said that’s what a true Arab would say. Today the headlines clot in my blood. A little Palestinian dangles a truck on the front page. Homeless fig, this tragedy with a terrible root is too big for us. What flag can we wave? I wave the flag of stone and seed, table mat stitched in blue. I call my father, we talk around the news. It is too much for him, neither of his two languages can reach it. I drive into the country to find sheep, cows, to plead with the air: Who calls anyone civilized? Where can the crying heart graze? What does a true Arab do now?

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Arab, And, True

outputs.L1:
“My father would say, ‘A true Arab knows how to catch a fly in his hands.’ Then he would prove it, cupping the buzzing thing in an instant while the host stood staring, swatter in hand. In spring, our palms peeled like snakes. True Arabs believed watermelon could heal in fifty different ways. I changed these sayings to suit the occasion.

Years earlier, a girl knocked on our door and asked to see the Arab. I told her we didn’t have one. After that, my father told me who he was: ‘Shihab’—‘shooting star’—a good name, borrowed from the sky. Once I asked, ‘When we die, do we give it back?’ He said that was exactly what a true Arab would say.

Today, the headlines clot in my blood. On the front page, a little Palestinian dangles a truck. Homeless fig, this tragedy, with its terrible root, is too large for us. What flag can we wave? I wave the flag of stone and seed, a table mat stitched in blue. I call my father, and we talk around the news. It is too much for him; neither of his two languages can reach it.

I drive into the country to find sheep and cows, to plead with the air: Who calls anyone civilized? Where can the crying heart graze? What does a true Arab do now?”
outputs.L2: “My father used to tell me, ‘A real Arab can trap a fly with his bare hands.’ Then he would demonstrate, closing his palms around the buzzing insect before the person holding the flyswatter could even react. In springtime, the skin on our hands came off in strips, like a snake shedding. Real Arabs, he said, knew watermelon had fifty kinds of healing power. I altered such sayings depending on the moment. Long ago, a girl came to the door asking to look at the Arab. I told her there wasn’t one in our house. Afterward, my father explained who he was: ‘Shihab,’ meaning ‘shooting star’—a fine name taken from the heavens. Once I asked, ‘When we die, do we return it?’ He told me that was exactly the sort of thing a true Arab would say. Now the news thickens inside my blood. On the front page, a small Palestinian child holds a toy truck. Rootless fig, this sorrow, with its dreadful buried cause, is more than we can bear. What banner is there for us to lift? I raise the banner of stone and seed, a blue-stitched table covering. I telephone my father, and we speak carefully around the headlines. The grief is beyond him; neither of the two languages he knows can contain it. I drive out toward the countryside, searching for sheep and cattle, begging the air for answers: Who has the right to call anyone civilized? Where is there pasture for a heart that weeps? What is a true Arab supposed to do now?”
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on her father’s teachings about Arab identity, remembering the sayings and demonstrations through which he tried to define what “a true Arab” knows and believes. His lessons are both practical and symbolic, suggesting that identity is not only inherited but also shaped through language, memory, values, and behavior. Through his words, the father passes down a sense of cultural pride and responsibility.

As a child, however, the speaker experiences confusion and shame about being Arab. She does not fully understand what this identity means or how to carry it in a world that may misunderstand or stereotype it. This uncertainty begins to change when she learns her father’s name, “Shihab,” and discovers that it means “shooting star.” The meaning of the name gives her a new way to understand her heritage. Instead of feeling only embarrassment or confusion, she begins to see Arab identity as something luminous, powerful, and connected to the vastness of the sky.

The image of the shooting star becomes an important symbol in the poem. It links the father to beauty, movement, and light, while also connecting the speaker’s identity to something larger than national borders or political labels. The sky suggests a shared human space, but it also becomes a place where memory and ancestry are preserved. Through her father’s name, the speaker finds a source of pride and a deeper connection to her roots.

At the same time, the speaker is deeply shaken by news of Palestinian suffering. The scale of violence and grief feels too immense to be represented by ordinary symbols such as flags. A flag may stand for a nation, but it cannot fully contain the pain of displacement, death, and historical trauma. The speaker’s emotional response reveals how personal identity is tied to collective suffering. Her Arab identity is not abstract; it is bound up with the real experiences of people enduring loss and injustice.

By the end of the poem, the speaker is left with difficult questions. She wonders what it truly means to be “civilized” when the world allows such suffering to continue. She also questions what a “true Arab” should do when confronted with grief, violence, and helplessness. Rather than offering a simple answer, the poem ends in uncertainty, suggesting that identity involves not only pride and memory but also moral responsibility, compassion, and the burden of witnessing pain.
outputs.L4:
Arab identity is not presented as a simple inheritance, a flag, a language, or a name carried proudly from one generation to the next. It appears instead as something troubled, intimate, and wounded, passed down through fragments: a father’s stories, old sayings, remembered gestures, and the quiet weight of historical loss. The speaker’s sense of self is shaped by family memory as much as by politics. The father becomes a central figure, not only as a parent but as a bearer of an older world — a world of customs, phrases, disappointments, and forms of endurance. Through him, identity is shown to be both personal and collective, something lived at the dinner table and in exile, in jokes and warnings, in affection and silence.

Cultural sayings and inherited expressions carry great importance in the text. They seem at first to offer wisdom, continuity, and belonging. They connect the speaker to a wider Arab past and to the shared habits of a people who have survived displacement, humiliation, and repeated catastrophe. Yet these sayings also reveal their limits. In the face of Palestinian suffering, language begins to falter. Proverbs, patriotic phrases, and inherited ideas about honor or civilization can no longer fully explain what has happened. They may comfort, but they cannot repair. They may preserve memory, but they cannot undo loss.

The suffering of Palestinians becomes the emotional and moral center of the reflection. It is not treated as an abstract political issue but as a wound that changes the meaning of everything around it. The speaker confronts the pain of a people whose homes, names, histories, and futures have been repeatedly threatened or destroyed. This tragedy presses against every attempt to define identity. What does it mean to belong to a culture when that culture is marked by grief? What does it mean to speak of dignity when people are denied safety, land, and recognition? What does it mean to call oneself civilized when civilization itself has allowed, excused, or ignored such suffering?

As the text develops, the speaker becomes increasingly uncertain about inherited definitions of pride and belonging. Arab identity is not rejected, but it is questioned. It is no longer enough to claim a noble history, a beautiful language, or a shared cultural memory. The speaker senses that identity must be measured against suffering: against how people respond to injustice, how they remember the dead, and how they carry the pain of others. Political tragedy overwhelms ordinary language because the scale of grief is too large for easy explanation. Words such as “honor,” “homeland,” “civilization,” and even “truth” begin to feel unstable.

The father’s presence deepens this conflict. He represents continuity, but also helplessness. His anecdotes and sayings link the speaker to the past, yet they also expose the burden of that past. Through him, the speaker understands that memory is not only a source of pride; it is also a form of inheritance that can ache. To remember is to belong, but it is also to suffer. The father’s world has given the speaker a language, but that language is strained by history. It cannot fully contain the sorrow of Palestine or the contradictions of Arab existence in a world shaped by defeat, exile, and longing.

Ultimately, the text becomes a meditation on what “true” identity can mean when identity itself has been wounded. The speaker does not arrive at a simple answer. Instead, the text remains in a state of questioning. Perhaps dignity lies not in grand declarations but in refusing to forget. Perhaps civilization is not measured by power or refinement, but by the ability to recognize another people’s pain. Perhaps true identity is not something pure or fixed, but something formed through memory, grief, responsibility, and love.

In this way, the text explores Arab identity as a deeply human struggle. It shows how personal memory and political tragedy cannot be separated, how the father’s voice and the suffering of Palestine echo within the same emotional landscape. Belonging is not easy; it is filled with sorrow, contradiction, and doubt. Yet the act of questioning itself becomes meaningful. By asking what dignity, civilization, and identity mean in the face of grief, the speaker refuses empty pride and searches instead for a more honest way to remember, to belong, and to speak.
outputs.L5:
Arab culture is rich with history, language, art, and tradition. From ancient poetry to modern innovation, Arab communities have contributed greatly to science, literature, architecture, and philosophy. Their stories reflect resilience, creativity, and a deep connection to heritage.

And throughout history, cultural exchange has helped people understand one another better. When traditions are shared with respect, they build bridges between communities and encourage peace.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical first-person prose poem about Arab American identity, a father’s sayings, inherited culture, and the grief of reading news about Palestine, ending with a question about what it means to be a “true Arab” now.
counterfactuals.output:
My father says, *don’t forget where you come from*, as if the place were a coin tucked under my tongue, as if I could open my mouth and pay the ferryman in olive pits, coffee grounds, the names of villages my American teachers could not pronounce. He says, *your blood knows*, and I want to ask him what blood knows after airports, after hyphens, after the shame of correcting someone gently and then not correcting them at all. He says, *we are a people of generosity*, and I see his hands arranging fruit for guests who have already eaten, pressing seconds onto plates, breaking bread like a small, daily resurrection.

I inherited more than language. I inherited the ache of it. The Arabic I have is a room with several locked doors, but I still know how to knock. I know the music of my aunties’ laughter rising over cardamom and smoke, the blue eye pinned above a doorway, the embroidered dress in the closet like a field remembered by thread. I know how the men lower their voices when they speak of land. I know how the women carry history without calling it history, in recipes, in mourning songs, in the way they say *come in, come in* even when the house is full.

And then the news arrives, glowing in my palm like a wound that learned electricity. Palestine scrolls past me in ruins and names, in mothers lifting dust from the faces of children, in men searching rubble as if the earth might give back what it swallowed. I sit in a quiet American room with a full glass of water and feel grief become a second skeleton. What good is my sorrow from so far away? What good is my remembering, my reposting, my candle, my cracked prayer? Still, I read because to look away feels like another kind of exile. Still, I whisper the names I can, because a name is a house no bomb can fully destroy.

My father says, *hold your head high*. He says, *never be ashamed*. But shame is not always ours, and still it finds us. It is in the questions asked too loudly, in the silence after I say Arab, in the way the world demands our grief be footnoted, balanced, made palatable. I carry my father’s sayings like beads in my pocket, rubbing them smooth: *be kind, be proud, remember, endure*. I carry a homeland I have touched only in fragments. I carry America too, its highways and winter coats, its promises with teeth.

Some days I am all inheritance; some days I am only longing dressed in borrowed grammar. Some days I hear my father’s voice and feel the old trees inside me lift their leaves. Some days the news turns every word to ash, and I do not know how to be worthy of the dead, the living, the scattered, the steadfast. I only know I am still listening—to the coffee boiling over, to the prayer my grandmother folded into my name, to the sea between us, to the rubble speaking.

And if my father’s voice is a lantern, and Palestine a grief that will not let me sleep, and America the place where I learned to explain myself, then tell me: what does it mean to be a true Arab now?
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short creative nonfiction piece in the style of Naomi Shihab Nye, weaving childhood memories, an Arab father, symbolic objects like watermelon, figs, stones, and seeds, and a response to Middle East violence in the news.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Naomi Shihab Nye’s exact style, but here is an original short creative nonfiction piece that draws on related themes: childhood, an Arab father, ordinary objects, tenderness, and grief in response to violence.

---

My father cut watermelon as if opening a country.

He laid the knife down first, flat beside the fruit, and studied the green globe on the kitchen table. I was seven, barefoot, my knees dusty from the yard. Outside, the hose ticked against the grass. Inside, my father pressed one broad hand to the rind and said, “Listen.”

I leaned close.

There was no sound I could hear, only the small thump of his knuckles testing sweetness. But he nodded as if the melon had answered in Arabic, a language I understood in pieces: bread, moon, wait, come here, enough.

When he split it open, the red flesh startled me every time. A hidden flag. A summer heart. Seeds shone black as tiny eyes.

“Don’t swallow them,” my cousin said. “A vine will grow inside you.”

My father smiled. “There are worse things to grow inside a person.”

He meant kindness, maybe. Or patience. Or a country you had never seen but were expected to love.

In the fall, figs appeared in a blue bowl on the counter, soft and wrinkled, purple-brown, their skins splitting at the top like tired mouths. My father ate them slowly, with respect. He told me his mother had dried figs on the roof, turning them each day in the sun. He said the roof was white, the stones around the house were white, the road was dust, and the sky was so large it made a person honest.

On the news now, the same sky fills with smoke.

I am older than my father was in those stories, older than the hands that lifted figs from a rooftop. I sit at my own table while the television offers numbers: dead, wounded, missing. The words arrive clean and cold. They do not show the boy who kept a smooth stone in his pocket because it looked like an egg. They do not show the mother saving seeds in a folded paper packet. They do not show a father slicing watermelon for children who will remember the red of it years later and feel ashamed of how beautiful anything can be while other people are afraid.

When the images become too much, I go outside and pick up stones from the edge of the garden. Small ones, ordinary ones, gray and tan and rust-colored. My father taught me stones are never empty. They remember pressure, weather, footsteps, the heat of old afternoons. I line them along the windowsill. I don’t know what else to do.

Then I rinse a handful of seeds from a melon and set them on a napkin to dry.

They look like punctuation marks from a sentence no one has finished.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a poetic monologue from the perspective of an Arab American speaker reflecting on family stories, language, names, and helplessness in the face of Palestinian suffering.
counterfactuals.output:
I carry my family in mismatched syllables—  
names softened at borders,  
creased by teachers’ mouths,  
folded small enough to fit inside a form.

My grandmother’s village arrives to me  
in fragments:  
a fig tree, a key,  
the blue eye of an amulet,  
bread rising under a cloth,  
a cousin’s laughter lost in the static  
between countries.

I was raised with stories  
that began before I did,  
stories that crossed oceans  
without luggage,  
stories my parents offered carefully,  
as if memory were a glass cup  
and I was always too young  
to hold it.

Arabic came to me like rain  
on a window—  
near enough to hear,  
too blurred to fully enter.  
I know the language of greetings,  
of grief,  
of food passed from hand to hand.  
I know how my name sounds  
when my mother says it:  
not strange,  
not difficult,  
not something needing explanation.

But outside our home  
my name became a question.  
It was trimmed, translated,  
made convenient.  
I learned to answer quickly,  
to laugh before anyone could stumble,  
to make my mouth a bridge  
and let others cross me.

Now I watch Palestine  
through the terrible glow of a screen,  
and every word I have  
feels too small,  
a cup of water held out  
to a burning house.

Children become numbers.  
Mothers become headlines.  
Fathers dig with their hands.  
The sky, so often praised in poems,  
opens and opens  
and will not stop falling.

What can I do  
with my safe kitchen,  
my clean tap water,  
my passport,  
my trembling thumb  
scrolling past ruins  
that look like they are asking me  
to remember them correctly?

I say their names when I can.  
I let the consonants stay sharp.  
I refuse to make the dead easy.  
I refuse to call sorrow complicated  
when a child is pulled from dust.

Still, helplessness sits beside me  
like an old relative  
who will not leave.  
It drinks my coffee.  
It sleeps at the foot of my bed.  
It says: You are far away.  
It says: You are not enough.

And maybe I am not.  
Maybe none of us are, alone.

But my family taught me  
that a story can survive  
longer than a wall,  
that a name can be a homeland  
when the map is denied,  
that language, even broken,  
can carry bread,  
can carry mourning,  
can carry a key  
from one generation’s palm  
to the next.

So I speak—  
not because speaking saves,  
not because poetry is shelter,  
not because grief becomes lighter  
when given music—

but because silence  
has always been too willing  
to serve the powerful.

I speak because somewhere  
a grandmother is still saying  
the old names of trees.  
Because somewhere  
a child deserves morning  
without thunder.  
Because somewhere  
the sea is waiting  
to be seen  
without barbed wire in the mind.

And because my own name,  
after all these years,  
is still learning  
how to come home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a compressed, image-rich essay that begins with the line “A true Arab knows how to catch a fly in his hands” and moves from humorous childhood anecdotes to political grief and questions of civilization.
counterfactuals.output:
“A true Arab knows how to catch a fly in his hands”

My father said this in the kitchen, solemn as a judge, while a bluebottle circled the fruit bowl like a tiny bomber. I was six, sticky with watermelon, convinced that nationhood had finally been explained to me: not flags, not hymns, not the stern portraits hanging in barbershops, but the sudden clap of two hands around a speck of living noise. He held his fists together, shook them near my ear, and the trapped fly buzzed like an electric secret. Then he opened his palms and it escaped. “Mercy,” he said, as if adding an article to a constitution.

Childhood was full of such miniature civics. My grandmother measured rice by instinct and sorrow, never by cup. My uncle could fix a radio with a butter knife and a curse. The women on the balcony shouted down recipes, warnings, scandals, weather reports, and the occasional theology. A slipper flew with the accuracy of a guided missile. Pomegranates cracked open like red clocks. The adults laughed from the belly, argued from the throat, loved from the wound.

We children learned the map first as a series of prohibitions: don’t go near the checkpoint; don’t repeat what your teacher said; don’t ask why that cousin has no country on his passport; don’t point at the soldiers; don’t cry when the electricity dies. The world entered our house in fragments—grainy television footage, a martyr’s photograph taped to a shop window, a mother ululating until the sound broke and became animal. Still, someone always made tea. Still, someone peeled cucumbers into perfect green ribbons. Still, a fly found the sugar bowl.

Humor was our first shelter: jokes told during curfew, jokes about presidents, jokes about hunger so sharp they could slice bread. But grief waited beneath them, patient and state-sponsored. It sat at weddings. It occupied the spare chair. It knew the names of prisons, camps, disappeared men, bombed neighborhoods, treaties signed in expensive rooms by hands that had never dusted concrete from a child’s hair.

What is civilization, then? The museum or the breadline? The city of poets or the city under siege? The manuscript illuminated in gold, or the grandmother who hides the family deed in a flour tin because history keeps arriving with bulldozers? Perhaps civilization is not the empire that writes the law, but the hand that releases the fly. The hand that, despite humiliation, refuses to become only a fist.

And yet I do not want mercy to be demanded only from the wounded. I want it built into bridges, courts, borders, schools. I want a civilization that can hear a child laughing in a kitchen and consider that sound sacred infrastructure. I want one where no people must prove their humanity by surviving beautifully.

My father is older now. His hands tremble. Flies come and go through the open window, drunk on summer fruit. He watches them, smiling, and no longer bothers to catch them. “Let them live,” he says.

Outside, nations roar. Inside, the tea darkens. Somewhere, a small wing beats against the glass, asking what all our walls are for.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary prose poem about diaspora and heritage, including a father named Shihab, a childhood encounter with someone asking to “see the Arab,” and the speaker’s attempt to process tragic headlines from Palestine.
counterfactuals.output:
My father, Shihab, taught me that a name can be both lantern and suitcase—something you carry through airports, through classrooms, through the long fluorescent corridors of other people’s assumptions. He said our people learned to fold home small enough to fit inside the mouth: a few spices, a prayer, the blue rumor of the sea, the olive tree rehearsing patience in the blood.

When I was a child, someone knocked at the door and asked to “see the Arab,” as if I were an exhibit, a rare animal, a country behind glass. I remember standing there with my hair unbrushed, holding a plastic cup of juice, feeling the room tilt toward history. I did not yet know how many centuries can gather inside a child’s silence. I did not know I would spend years answering a question no one had earned the right to ask.

Now the headlines arrive each morning like broken dishes. Palestine again, Palestine still—names scrolling past before coffee, buildings opened to the sky, mothers lifting dust from faces, fathers carrying what no father should have to carry. I try to read without turning away. I try to turn away without becoming stone. My phone glows in my hand like a small, cruel moon, and I think of my father, Shihab, whose name means shooting star, whose grief was often quiet, practical: fix the hinge, slice the fruit, call your aunt, remember where you come from.

Heritage is not a costume I put on for festivals. It is the ache under ordinary speech. It is the way I flinch when strangers pronounce the world as if it belongs only to them. It is bread torn by hand, coffee bitter with cardamom, the old songs rising from someone’s kitchen, the map that keeps changing shape but not disappearing. It is being asked to prove your humanity in a language that has already misnamed you.

I keep trying to make a room inside myself large enough for all of it: the child at the door, the father with his star-name, the ancestors crossing water with keys and recipes, the dead whose photographs keep becoming public evidence. Some days I fail. Some days I can only whisper Palestine as if it were a wound and a promise, a place and a people and a word the world keeps trying to bury before it has finished breathing.

But my father says, remember. So I do. I remember forward. I carry the lantern.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
